title: India–USA

cards.h: The relationship that decides the rest
cards.b:
India–USA is the most-asked bilateral topic after China. It sits behind almost every other question in Paper II: the Indo-Pacific, Russia, nuclear policy, West Asia and the Global South.

The story has three layers. First, estrangement in the Cold War. Second, a strategic turn after 1998 and the 2005–08 nuclear deal. Third, a stress test in 2025–26 when tariffs, Russian oil and Trump's claims about Kashmir and Pakistan hit trust.

The best exam answers show both sides: the deep, institutional partnership and the real limits set by India's strategic autonomy.

Everything time-sensitive in this lesson is written "as of 2026". Check the latest news before the exam.

Why did two democracies drift apart? The US saw India's non-alignment as pro-Soviet. India saw US military aid to Pakistan as a threat. Nuclear policy added a second wall: the US led the non-proliferation regime India rejected.

The hinge was 1991. The Soviet Union fell and India liberalised. In 1998 the US imposed sanctions after Pokhran-II. But the Jaswant Singh–Strobe Talbott talks that followed began a real strategic dialogue.

cards.h: From Clinton to the civil nuclear deal
cards.b:
Bill Clinton's visit in March 2000 was the first US presidential visit in 22 years. In 2001 George W. Bush lifted the sanctions. In 2004 came the Next Steps in Strategic Partnership (NSSP).

The July 2005 joint statement (Manmohan Singh and Bush) set up the civil nuclear deal. The US passed the Hyde Act (2006). India and the IAEA agreed a safeguards deal. The Nuclear Suppliers Group gave India a clean waiver on 6 September 2008. The 123 Agreement was signed on 10 October 2008.

The deal ended India's nuclear isolation without India signing the NPT. It cost political capital: the Left withdrew support from the UPA government in July 2008.

US arms sales to India were close to zero in 2000. They have since grown into billions of dollars (P-8I, C-17, C-130J, Apache, Chinook, MQ-9B drones).

The US named India a Major Defense Partner in 2016. India signed the foundational agreements:

  • GSOMIA (2002): sharing of classified information.
  • LEMOA (2016): logistics support at each other's bases.
  • COMCASA (2018): secure military communications.
  • BECA (2020): geospatial data for targeting and navigation.

Exercises include Yudh Abhyas (army), Malabar (navy, with Japan and Australia) and Cope India (air). A 2+2 ministerial dialogue began in 2018. A new 10-year defence framework was signed on 31 October 2025 in Kuala Lumpur.

The Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) began in 2023 under Biden. In 2025 it was folded into the TRUST initiative (Transforming the Relationship Utilising Strategic Technology). Themes: semiconductors, AI, space, quantum and defence co-production such as the GE F414 jet engine.

Trade: the US is India's largest trading partner in goods, about $130 billion in 2024. India exported roughly $87 billion in FY2024-25 and runs a surplus. In February 2025 the two leaders set a target of $500 billion in trade by 2030.

People: about five million Indian Americans form one of the richest immigrant groups in the US. Indian students and H-1B workers are a major pillar. A $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions announced in September 2025 hit this pillar.

In 2025 the relationship faced its worst stress in decades.

  • Tariffs: a 25% 'reciprocal' tariff took effect on 7 August 2025. A further 25% penalty for buying Russian oil followed on 27 August. Total: 50%, among the highest on any US partner.
  • Ceasefire claims: after Operation Sindoor (7–10 May 2025), Trump repeatedly said he brokered the India–Pakistan ceasefire. India said it was agreed directly between the two DGMOs and rejected any mediation. Pakistan thanked Trump.
  • Pakistan outreach: Trump hosted Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and praised Pakistan.

India's reply was to keep strategic autonomy: it refused to stop Russian oil on command, hosted Putin in December 2025 and attended the SCO summit in Tianjin in 2025.

On 6 February 2026 the two governments announced a framework for an interim trade deal. The US said it would cut tariffs on India to 18% and remove the extra 25% Russian-oil penalty from 7 February.

Then the courts intervened. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court held that the IEEPA law does not authorise such tariffs. The administration shifted to other laws. The US then used temporary tariffs and opened Section 301 investigations in March 2026. As of late 2026, the final tariff rate and the signing of the deal were still not settled.

As of November 2026 there is still no signed treaty text and no entry-into-force date. Sticking points are agriculture and dairy, where India protects small farmers, and digital rules.

On Russian oil, Washington says India agreed to cut; trade data show Russian crude still arriving in 2026, though below the 2025 peak.

Realists (such as C. Raja Mohan) argue India must drop its Cold War caution and use the US to balance China. Autonomists (the Non-Alignment 2.0 report of 2012) warn against becoming a junior partner.

S. Jaishankar describes the current line as multi-alignment. India works with the US in the Quad and I2U2, with Russia in BRICS and SCO, and with Europe and the Gulf. India calls the US a "partner" but never an "ally": no treaty, no bases, no obligation to fight.

Structural irritants: CAATSA sanctions (2017) over the S-400, US positions on human rights, the Pannun plot case (2023), Pakistan, and trade protection.

Gains: technology, capital, defence co-production, an Indo-Pacific counterweight to China, a big market for services and a diaspora of about five million Indian Americans.

Risks: India becomes dependent on US tech controls. Tariff shocks hit labour-intensive sectors like textiles, gems and shrimp. US policy swings with each presidency. A US–China deal could leave India exposed.

India's response in 2025–26: diversify. It signed an FTA with the UK (July 2025), concluded one with the EU (January 2026), closed the EFTA agreement (2024, in force October 2025), and stayed in BRICS. It also kept buying US energy and defence goods to reduce the trade surplus.

For the exam, give one hard fact per claim: the 2008 NSG waiver, the 2016 Major Defense Partner label, the 50% tariff of 2025, and the 2026 framework.

"Discuss the significance of the Indo-US civil nuclear deal for India." (typical)
"India–US relations have moved from estrangement to engagement. Critically examine." (typical)
"Examine how the Quad and the Indo-Pacific shape India-US strategic convergence." (typical)

Structure: (1) Cold War estrangement; (2) post-1998 turn: NSSP, 2005 statement, 2008 deal; (3) pillars: defence, technology, trade, people, Indo-Pacific; (4) 2025–26 strain: tariffs, Russian oil, H-1B, Sindoor claims; (5) assessment: convergence on China, divergence on autonomy; (6) way forward: trade deal, co-production, diversification.

Always name at least three dates and two agreements.

quiz.q: Which law passed by the US Congress in 2006 enabled the civil nuclear cooperation with India?
quiz.w: The Henry J. Hyde United States-India Peaceful Atomic Energy Cooperation Act (2006) enabled the deal.

quiz.q: The NSG granted India a clean waiver on:
quiz.w: The NSG waiver was granted on 6 September 2008. The 123 Agreement was signed on 10 October 2008.

quiz.q: Which foundational agreement provides for geospatial data sharing, signed in 2020?
quiz.w: BECA (Basic Exchange and Cooperation Agreement) covers geospatial cooperation.

quiz.q: The US gave India the label 'Major Defense Partner' in:
quiz.w: The designation came in June 2016, during Obama's presidency.

quiz.q: The Next Steps in Strategic Partnership (NSSP) was launched in:
quiz.w: NSSP was announced in January 2004 under Vajpayee and Bush.

quiz.q: The combined US tariff on most Indian goods from 27 August 2025 was:
quiz.w: 25% reciprocal plus 25% penalty linked to Russian oil gave 50%.

quiz.q: India's stated position on Trump's claim of mediating the May 2025 ceasefire was that:
o: The understanding was reached directly between DGMOs
quiz.w: India said it was a bilateral understanding via DGMO hotline and rejected mediation.

quiz.q: In February 2026 the US Supreme Court held that:
o: The tariff on India was legal
quiz.w: The Court ruled the IEEPA law did not authorise the tariffs.

quiz.q: The Pokhran-II tests that triggered US sanctions took place in:
'Multi-alignment' as a description of Indian policy is associated with:
quiz.w: Jaishankar popularised it in The India Way (2020) and speeches.
